subject: type names for constrained matrices & Cholesky factors

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: type names for constrained matrices & Cholesky factors
parts:
Right now, we have:

cov_matrix
corr_matrix
cholesky_factor_cov
cholesky_factor_corr [new!]

Ben pointed out "cov" is not general enough --- it's any
symmetric, positive definite matrix, including precision matrices.
Also, I was inconsistent in putting the modifier at the start
of cov_matrix but at the end of cholesky_factor_cov.

How about changing these (following previous discussion) to
follow Marcus's terminology in the API, where "spd" stands
for "symmetric, positive definite":

spd_matrix
corr_matrix
spd_cholesky
corr_cholesky

or to:

matrix_spd
matrix_corr
cholesky_spd
cholesky_corr

or be even more fully qualified:

matrix
matrix_spd
matrix_spd_unit_diag
matrix_cholesky_spd
matrix_cholesky_spd_unit_diag

Note that this drops "_factor" from "cholesky_factor".

I'll deprecate the existing ones and give users warnings to change
their usage.

I'm hoping it's OK with everyone if the new type goes in after 2.1.0.
We're trying to periodically freeze features and then do releases.

I'm working on branch:

feature/issue-413-cholesky-corr-type

to add the corr_cholesky type. (Thanks for the factor function, Ben --- that
was all I needed --- I'm about to test everything now in the square
case.)

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: type names for constrained matrices & Cholesky factors
parts:
On Saturday, December 7, 2013 5:12:28 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Right now, we have:

   cov_matrix
   corr_matrix
   cholesky_factor_cov
   cholesky_factor_corr    [new!]

Ben pointed out "cov" is not general enough --- it's any
symmetric, positive definite matrix, including precision matrices.
Also, I was inconsistent in putting the modifier at the start
of cov_matrix but at the end of cholesky_factor_cov.

How about changing these (following previous discussion) to
follow Marcus's terminology in the API, where "spd" stands
for "symmetric, positive definite":

spd is a good convention, but

   spd_matrix
   corr_matrix
   spd_cholesky
   corr_cholesky

spd_cholesky is not good. The Cholesky factor itself is not spd and the matrix that it is a Cholesky factor of is spd by construction.

or to:

   matrix_spd
   matrix_corr
   cholesky_spd
   cholesky_corr

I do think it makes more sense for the cholesky_ to come first, since in English we usually say that "L is the Cholesky factor of Sigma" rather than "Sigma's Cholesky factor is L". But by that logic, matrix_spd and matrix_corr sound backwards.

or be even more fully qualified:

   matrix
   matrix_spd
   matrix_spd_unit_diag
   matrix_cholesky_spd
   matrix_cholesky_spd_unit_diag

These seem too verbose. And more Stan users are more likely to understand what a corr_matrix is than to know that a matrix_spd_unit_diag is a correlation matrix.

In other words, corr_matrix was always unambiguous, although we need something unambiguous to refer to its Cholesky factor. But cov_matrix was misleading because it was never required to actually be a covariance matrix. So, having spd_matrix subsume cov_matrix is fine, I think.

Note that this drops "_factor" from "cholesky_factor".

I'll deprecate the existing ones and give users warnings to change
their usage.

I'm hoping it's OK with everyone if the new type goes in after 2.1.0.
We're trying to periodically freeze features and then do releases.

I'm working on branch:

   feature/issue-413-cholesky-corr-type

to add the corr_cholesky type.  (Thanks for the factor function, Ben --- that
was all I needed --- I'm about to test everything now in the square
case.)

That is fine. We need to add some densities. And I also I came up with a construction of a Cholesky factor of a precision matrix whose inverse is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ(eta).

Ben

Verbose and redundant because there is no such thing as cholesky_factor_of_foo for foo != spd. It would be like having an eigenvalues_of_a_matrix() function instead of an eigenvalues() function that took a matrix.

So, I think it should be

> That is fine. We need to add some densities. And I also I came up with a construction of a Cholesky factor of a

Not exactly. We have the LKJ density of a correlation matrix given its Cholesky factor. That is mostly confusing but occasionally useful (if you need L in a subsequent calculation). What is more useful would be the density of a Cholesky factor whose tcrossprod() is a correlation matrix. That should replace the existing function.

But what I was referring to above is basically a density for the inverse of a correlation matrix, like wishart vs. inv_wishart.

Ben

On Saturday, December 7, 2013 8:46:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>      > That is fine. We need to add some densities. And I also I came up with a construction of a Cholesky factor of a
>      > precision matrix whose inverse is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ(eta).
>
>     Didn't we have the LKJ density of a Cholesky factor?  And wasn't it
>     just going to be taken out until we got the correlation matrix types in.
>
>
> Not exactly. We have the LKJ density of a correlation matrix given its Cholesky factor. That is mostly confusing but
> occasionally useful (if you need L in a subsequent calculation). What is more useful would be the density of a Cholesky
> factor whose tcrossprod() is a correlation matrix. That should replace the existing function.

I don't get the difference (in English or in formulas).

The lkj_corr_cholesky() density that we have now in develop / master only makes sense if eta != 1 and you need the Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix for some other calculation. So,

parameters {
  corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
}
model {
  matrix[K,K] L;
  L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
  // ... use L for something ...
  // now time for priors
}

At this point, it is wasteful to call lkj_corr(Sigma) because lkj_corr() calculates the Cholesky factorization of Sigma twice, once in doubles to verify that it is in fact a correlation matrix and once in vars to obtain the Cholesky factor that it passes to lkj_corr_cholesky_log to evaluate 2(eta - 1) times the log determinant of L, which is equal to (eta - 1) times the log determinant of Sigma. Since the user already has L in vars at this point, it is much faster to call L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(eta), which does not even waste time verifying that L is triangular (because I never meant for it to get exposed).

The way I always envisioned it would work, which should happen in 2 releases, was to have L be primitive. So, the user would write

parameters {
  cholesky_corr[K] L;
}
model {
  // ... use L for something ...
  // now time for priors
}

At this point, we need a prior on L, but a uniform prior on L does not imply a uniform prior on L * L'. So, in general we need a density that should probably be called lkj_cholesky_corr (and disappear the uber-confusing lkj_corr_choleksy density), that is the density of L that implies L * L' is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. Since

f(Sigma | eta) = constant * det(Sigma)^(eta - 1)

we make the change of variables Sigma = L * L' to get

f(L | eta) = constant * |det(J)| * det(L*L')^(eta - 1) = constant * |det(J)| * det(L)^(2 * eta - 2)

where J is the Jacobian matrix for the transformation from the strictly lower-triangular elements of L to the strictly lower-triangular elements of Sigma. Even though the Stan manual says that "the only description [of J] so far is in the Stan transform code", the Jacobian is triangular and its diagonal is not too hard to work out and only depends on the diagonal of L. So, now the user would use L ~ lkj_cholesky_corr(eta) and only calculate Sigma = L * L' in the generated quantities block if at all.

My understanding is that we want to be able to do something like
the following for efficiency:

   parameters {
     cholesky_corr[K] L_corr;
     vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
     ...

   model {
     matrix[K,K] L_cov;
     L_cov <- diag_matrix(sigma) * L_corr;

     L_corr ~ lkj_cholesky_corr(eta);
     sigma ~ ...

     for (n in 1:N)
       y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L_cov);
     ...

That is more efficient, but not optimally efficient because multi_normal_cholesky has to triangular solve L_cov * x = (y[n] - mu). Marcus put the inverse of L_cov on the heap so that you don't have do the hard part of the triangular solve N times. But what you really want is to not have to do that at all, and use the (as yet non-existent) density multi_normal_cholesky_prec density where you supply the Cholesky factor of an unknown precision matrix. So, you want to know the (Cholesky factor of a) precision matrix whose inverse is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta and maybe you can scale that precision matrix from both sides by a diagonal matrix of reciprocal standard deviations. This might look like

parameters {
  cholesky_corr[K] L;
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma;
}
model {
  matrix[K,K] L_prec;
  vector[K] D;
  D <- figure_out_D(L);
  // Sigma = inverse(diag_matrix(D) * L * L' * diag_matrix(D)) is a correlation matrix
  L_prec <- diag_matrix(ones ./ (D * sigma)) * L
  for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky_prec(mu,L_prec);
  // now time for priors
}

Here you need the prior on L that would imply that Sigma is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. Again, since

f(Sigma | eta) = constant * det(Sigma)^(eta - 1)

we can make the change of variables Sigma_inv = inverse(Sigma) so that

f(Sigma_inv | eta) = constant * |det(J)| * det(inverse(Sigma_inv))^(eta - 1) = constant * |det(J)| * det(Sigma_inv)^(1-eta)

where J is the Jacobian matrix for the transformation from Sigma_inv to Sigma. That is not too hard and also involves the determinant of Sigma but is more complicated in this case because the diagonal of Sigma is not a random variable. But once you have the density for Sigma_inv = diag_matrix(D) * L * L' * diag_matrix(D), it should just be another change of variables to get the density for L.

In the end, the added analytical complication would only be worthwhile for large K, but figure_out_D() is only O(K^2).

Ben
